title: The Sea Inside
full_review:
In "The Sea Inside" (Fine Line), Javier Bardem, giving what is perhaps the standout performance of the year, plays real-life Spanish poet Ramon Sampedro, who, after a tragic diving accident at age 18 left him paralyzed from the neck down, fought a 30-year battle against Spain's legal system for the right to end his own life.

While wrestling with the thorny issue of euthanasia, director Alejandro Amenabar manages to navigate the film's moral minefield with a fair degree of objectivity resulting in a picture that -- though unavoidably controversial -- is nevertheless thought-provoking, compelling and hauntingly beautiful.

Soberly and sensitively crafted, "The Sea Inside" is, without a doubt, emotionally moving, yet never overly gloomy or heavy-handed in its sentimentality.

Confined to a bed in a rural region of Spain where he lives with his rough-hewn brother (Celso Bugallo), his elderly father (Joan Dalmau), his teenage nephew (Tamar Novas) and his dedicated sister-in-law caretaker (Mabel Rivera), Ramon relies on others for everything, from getting washed and dressed, to being fed, to -- if he had his way -- helping him kill himself.

Despite his broken body, the light of his mind remains undimmed. A natural poet, Ramon writes by using a stick he holds between his teeth. He also has a disarming smile and a wry sense of humor (in one scene he tells his nephew to make sure that his wheelchair is secure, joking "I wouldn't want to break my neck").

Ironically, his ability to instill a deeper appreciation for life in other people makes his decision to extinguish his own life all the more perplexing. Some viewers may, with some justification, see his suicidal solution as insensitive to family members who lovingly sacrificed so much to take care of him.

"The Sea Inside" focuses on Ramon's relationship with two women: a terminally ill lawyer (Belen Rueda) hired to help with his case and a lonely single mother (Lola Duenas) with whom he bonds.

Given the physical limitations demanded by the role, the range of emotions and personality that Bardem is able to convey using just his expressive eyes and minimal facial gestures is extraordinary. Makeup work by Jo Allen helped transform the robust 35-year-old Bardem into a graying man in his mid-50s, and the resulting illusion of age and infirmity is startlingly realistic.

The picture is full of dreamlike visuals including a fantasy sequence scored to Puccini 's "Nessun dorma," in which Ramon rises from his bed -- liberated from the prison of his body -- and flies out an open window, soaring euphorically over the Galician countryside to a turquoise sea.

Amenabar's film raises profound moral questions concerning death, dignity, the sanctity of human life and personal autonomy. Opinions will undoubtedly vary, with many viewers seeing the movie as little more than a gilded defense of assisted suicide, especially given its morally problematic ending.

The film clearly displays sympathies for those who hold the belief that, in an "enlightened" democratic society, people should have the right to terminate their lives if they so choose. However, Amenabar avoids outright advocacy for euthanasia, by allowing impassioned voices from both sides of the issue to be heard, including a local priest (Jose Maria Pou) -- also a quadriplegic -- who offers a spirited defense of the Catholic position, battling Ramon to a Socratic draw.

In another scene, Ramon's brother vehemently tries to open his son's eyes to the gravity of the situation unfolding: "Don't you know what happens if he wins the case? They give your uncle a shot and he dies! This is serious stuff!"

From a Catholic standpoint, what is objectionable is not that Amenabar has chosen to make a film dealing with assisted suicide, but that in doing so he seems to suggest -- borrowing language from the U.S. bishops' 1991 statement on euthanasia -- that self-autonomy is the highest good and "ultimate freedom," insisting that "the right to choose must prevail over all other considerations," a view distilled to the shibboleth "life is a right, not an obligation" repeated throughout the picture.

When asked "Why die?" Ramon responds, "because every journey has a departure and only the traveler has the right and privilege to choose the last day to get out." While viewers' sense of compassion might understandably incline them to empathize with Ramon's plight and deem his decision to "die with dignity" reasonable (i.e., "Isn't it cruel to prolong his suffering by asking him to soldier on?"), Catholic theology holds that life -- as the bishops' statement reminds us -- "is the most basic gift of a loving God ... (and that) a decision to takes one's life or to kill a suffering patient is very different from a decision to refuse extraordinary or disproportionately burdensome treatment."

And though it seems harsh to criticize someone in Ramon's condition, the church's teaching is clear: We are stewards, not owners, of the life God has entrusted to us. It is not ours to dispose of.

Because of a sympathetic view of euthanasia and some brief mild sensuality, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
